summary: Specifies the RPKI Repository Delta Protocol, which relying parties use to fetch published RPKI data over HTTPS. It uses an update notification file that lists a snapshot and deltas, and is designed to scale with caches and CDNs. Later RFCs update it.

plainLanguage.summary: RRDP lets RPKI relying parties download a complete repository snapshot or just the changes since their last update. A small notification file identifies the available files, which can be distributed and cached over HTTPS.

questions: what is an rpki update notification file
how often can rrdp be polled
subtitle: How RPKI relying parties retrieve repository snapshots and incremental changes over HTTPS.

tldr.problem: Rsync makes repository servers spend significant CPU and memory on each connection, which can burden a small number of repositories serving many relying parties.
tldr.mechanism: A repository publishes an Update Notification File that identifies the current snapshot and a contiguous set of deltas. Relying parties retrieve those immutable files over HTTPS and verify their hashes.
tldr.outcome: RRDP provides an additional distribution mechanism that can coexist with rsync and use caching infrastructure. RFC 8182 is updated by RFC 9674 and RFC 9697.

today: RFC 8182 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9674 and RFC 9697. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why RRDP Adds Another Repository Method
sections.content:
RPKI certificate authorities publish certificates, signed objects, manifests and CRLs to repositories. Relying parties retrieve those objects to validate RPKI data. Before RRDP, rsync was the repository access method.

The RFC describes concerns with rsync: a server uses significant CPU and memory for every connection, which can burden central repositories serving many relying parties. It also notes that supported client and server libraries are lacking, so implementations often call an external rsync program.

RRDP provides another way to retrieve repository data. It uses files over HTTPS that can be precomputed and distributed through caches or content distribution networks.
sections.plainLanguage: RRDP adds an HTTPS-based way for relying parties to retrieve RPKI repository data. Its files can be prepared once and served to many clients through caches.

sections.title: Notification, Snapshot and Delta Files
sections.content:
A certificate that supports RRDP includes an SIA pointer to an Update Notification File. The notification contains a session_id, a serial number, a link to the latest complete Snapshot File and links to available Delta Files.

A relying party seeing the location for the first time downloads the notification and snapshot, then records the location, session_id and serial. Later it checks the notification for a contiguous chain of deltas from its serial. If the session changes or the chain is incomplete, it resynchronizes from the snapshot.

Snapshots and deltas for a session and serial are immutable, so they can be cached indefinitely. The notification is polled for changes and should not be cached for longer than one minute.
sections.plainLanguage: A notification file points to a complete snapshot and to files containing later changes. A relying party applies a complete chain of changes or downloads a fresh snapshot if a change is missing.

sections.title: Publishing Repository Updates
sections.content:
When a repository server initializes, it creates a random version 4 UUID for the session and publishes a snapshot at serial 1. It then publishes a notification referring to that snapshot, with no delta files.

After receiving CA updates, the server must publish a new snapshot and delta within one minute. The new serial is exactly one greater than the previous serial. The delta contains the added, replaced and withdrawn objects for that update; the snapshot contains all current objects.

The server can combine updates from multiple CAs, but must not delay any CA's publication by more than one minute. If it cannot produce the required files, it must fully reinitialize the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Each repository change creates a new snapshot, a delta and a higher serial number. The server publishes those files and updates the notification within one minute.

sections.title: Applying Changes at a Relying Party
sections.content:
A relying party downloads and validates the notification file, then compares its session_id with the last one recorded for that file location. It must not use the session_id alone to identify a repository session, because a malicious server could reuse another server's value.

If the session matches and a contiguous delta chain is available, the relying party downloads deltas in serial order and checks each file's format, hash, session_id and next serial. Before applying a withdrawal or replacement, it must confirm the object came from the same repository server.

If any delta is missing or rejected, or the session_id changes, the relying party uses the snapshot instead and verifies its hash and serial. It must not poll more than once per minute and must use If-Modified-Since.
sections.plainLanguage: The relying party checks that each file matches the notification and continues the same repository sequence. If a delta fails a check, it discards the delta path and synchronizes from a complete snapshot.

sections.title: The XML File Structure
sections.content:
The notification, snapshot and delta are XML documents in the RRDP namespace. They use US-ASCII encoding and protocol version 1. A relying party must reject a file that is not well formed or does not conform to the RELAX NG schema.

The notification identifies its session and serial, contains exactly one snapshot reference and may contain delta references with SHA-256 hashes. The snapshot contains a publish element for each current object. A delta contains publish elements for new or replaced objects and withdraw elements for removed objects.

Snapshot and delta publish entries include the object's rsync URI. Snapshot content is base64 encoded. The notification's delta serials must form a contiguous sequence through the current serial, even if the elements are not listed in serial order.
sections.plainLanguage: The three RRDP files use a defined XML structure with version and session information. Their schema and hashes let a relying party reject files that are incomplete or inconsistent.

sections.title: Caching and Coexistence with Rsync
sections.content:
Snapshot and delta files do not change after publication, so a server or content distribution network can cache them. Repository servers should retain old snapshots and deltas for at least 5 minutes after they are no longer referenced, allowing clients that fetched a notification just before an update to retrieve the files.

Notification files are different because clients poll them for updates. They should not be cached for more than one minute. Relying parties must not poll more than once per minute and must use If-Modified-Since.

RRDP can coexist with rsync. The snapshot and delta entries include content hashes and rsync URIs, allowing the same repository objects to be distributed through both mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Unchanging snapshots and deltas can be served from caches, but the notification needs to stay fresh. RRDP can operate alongside rsync using the same repository objects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RPKI objects have their own signatures and validation rules, so a relying party can validate them without trusting the repository server. RRDP does not change RPKI object validation procedures.

HTTPS protects the channel and can make some denial-of-service attacks harder, but an on-path attacker can still withhold or replay data. Relying parties should check TLS certificates and hostnames, while continuing to retrieve the signed data if those checks fail so object validation can still proceed.

A malicious CA can provide many repository URIs through either RRDP or rsync. Relying parties therefore need limits on the work they are willing to perform. A delta is processed as a complete change set, which can avoid applying only part of an update.
sections.plainLanguage: Object signatures let relying parties detect invalid repository data even if they do not trust the server. HTTPS protects delivery but cannot stop an attacker from withholding or replaying files.

  <snapshot uri="https://host/9d-8/3/snapshot.xml" hash="AB"/>
  <delta serial="3" uri="https://host/9d-8/3/delta.xml" hash="CD"/>
  <delta serial="2" uri="https://host/9d-8/2/delta.xml" hash="EF"/>
</notification>
